title: Data Structures: Organizing Data for Speed

questions.question: Roughly how many steps does binary search take to find one item among a million?
questions.rationale: Each step halves the remaining candidates, and 2^20 exceeds 1,000,000 — so binary search needs about 20 comparisons versus up to a million for a linear scan.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of accessing the i-th element of an array versus a linked list?
options: O(n) for the array and O(1) for the list
O(1) for the array and O(n) for the list
questions.rationale: Arrays compute the element's address directly from the index (O(1)); a linked list must walk node by node from the head (O(n)).

questions.question: A data structure where the last element inserted is the first removed — used for undo and the function call stack — is a:
questions.rationale: A stack is LIFO (last in, first out) with O(1) push, pop, and peek; it backs function call stacks, undo, and browser back.

questions.question: In a hash table, what is a collision?
options: The table runs out of memory
Two different keys hash to the same bucket
A key is inserted twice with different values
The load factor drops below one
questions.rationale: A collision is two distinct keys mapping to the same index; it is handled by chaining (a list per bucket) or open addressing (probing for a free slot).

questions.question: What is the worst-case complexity of a hash table lookup?
questions.rationale: Average lookup is O(1), but if every key hashes to the same bucket the operation degenerates to scanning a list — O(n).

questions.question: Which traversal of a binary search tree visits keys in sorted order?
questions.rationale: In-order traversal — left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree — yields keys in ascending sorted order.

questions.question: Inserting the keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 into a plain BST in that order illustrates which hazard?
options: The tree degenerates into a linked list with O(n) search
Every insert causes a hash collision
The tree cannot store duplicates of itself
questions.rationale: Sorted insertion builds a right-leaning chain — effectively a linked list — so search degrades from O(log n) to O(n); self-balancing trees prevent this.

questions.question: Which pair correctly distinguishes AVL trees from red-black trees?
options: AVL trees are heaps; red-black trees are hash tables
AVL is strictly height-balanced; red-black uses looser color rules with fewer rotations (used in std::map)
Red-black trees cannot search by key; AVL trees cannot insert
Both are implemented only in Python
questions.rationale: AVL trees enforce sibling heights differing by at most 1; red-black trees use relaxed color invariants and fewer rotations, powering std::map and Java's TreeMap.

questions.question: Which structure is the natural engine for a priority queue that repeatedly extracts the smallest item?
options: A heap, with O(1) find-min and O(log n) delete-min
A plain array with O(1) find-min
A linked list with O(log n) find-min
questions.rationale: A min-heap keeps the smallest item at the root: peeking is O(1) and removing it is O(log n), which is exactly what priority queues, Dijkstra's algorithm, and heapsort need.

questions.question: Your program needs fast lookup by key AND the ability to list keys in sorted order. Which structure fits best?
questions.rationale: Hash tables forget order entirely; a balanced BST gives O(log n) keyed operations plus sorted in-order traversal and range queries.
